sponsor_and_incentive: None. WHO is the publisher and maintainer of ICD; no product sold. The statement says WHO is about to develop evidence-based guidelines on mental well-being in the workplace.
exact_quotes: WHO statement (28 May 2019): 'Burn-out is a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.' Characterised by three dimensions: 'feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion'; 'increased mental distance from one's job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism related to one's job'; and 'reduced professional efficacy'. Also: 'Burn-out refers specifically to phenomena in the occupational context and should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life.' The page states burn-out 'is not classified as a medical condition' and sits in the chapter on factors influencing health status or contact with health services. [uncertain: the fetch tool returned only fragments as quotes and paraphrased the rest, so the wording of dimensions 2 and the 'refers specifically' sentence is from the tool's summary plus snippets, not read on-screen by me]
date_and_recency: Statement published 28 May 2019 (ICD-11 adopted at the World Health Assembly that month; in force 1 January 2022). WHO page footer showed a 2026 copyright and a related 'Mental health at work' fact sheet dated 15 September 2026. ICD browser release consulted: 2025-01.
key_claims: Burn-out is included in ICD-11 as an 'occupational phenomenon', not a medical condition. It is defined as a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Three dimensions: exhaustion; mental distance, cynicism or negativism toward one's job; reduced professional efficacy. It applies only to the occupational context. ICD-10 also included burn-out in a similar category, with a less detailed definition.
headline_figures: No numeric figures. ICD-11 code QD85. Statement dated 28 May 2019.
sample_unit_and_population: Not an empirical study; a classification definition. No sample. Not specific to software engineers; applies to any occupation.
observed_vs_stated: Neither. Conceptual and classificatory definition by WHO.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Defines burn-out as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with three dimensions: energy depletion or exhaustion; increased mental distance from the job or negativism/cynicism about it; reduced professional efficacy. It is a definition, not a measurement instrument.
mechanism_or_cause: Chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. No detailed mechanism given. The statement does not name specific workplace causes.
interventions_and_effects: None tested or recommended in the statement. WHO says it is about to develop evidence-based guidelines on mental well-being in the workplace. No effect sizes.
transfer_to_software_teams: Occupation-neutral definition, so it applies to software teams by default; it offers no software-specific evidence.
limitations_stated: WHO restricts the term to the occupational context: it 'should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life.' It is classed as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. The ICD-11 entry (QD85) lists exclusions: adjustment disorder (6B43), disorders specifically associated with stress (6B40-6B4Z), anxiety or fear-related disorders (6B00-6B0Z), mood disorders (6A60-6A8Z). [uncertain: exclusion list taken from mirror sites, not WHO's own rendered page]
counter_evidence: Press at the time widely misreported the decision as burnout becoming an official 'medical condition' or 'diagnosis'; WHO's wording says the opposite. Wider literature disputes overlap between burnout and depression, but that is not covered in this source and was not checked here. [uncertain]
verification_status: Definition, three dimensions, 'not a medical condition' and occupational-context restriction: checked against the opened WHO 2019 page (via fetch tool summary). Exclusion list and QD85 placement: NOT checked against WHO's ICD browser; third-party mirrors only. [uncertain]
usable_claim: WHO's ICD-11 describes burn-out as an occupational phenomenon, a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. WHO says it is not classified as a medical condition and applies only to work.
do_not_use: Do not say WHO recognised burnout as a medical condition or illness. Do not apply the three dimensions to life outside work. Do not cite the exclusion list as WHO-verified until QD85 is opened at icd.who.int. Do not imply WHO identifies causes specific to software work.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the essays 'Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part', the trust essay or 'Checking Isn't Catching'. [uncertain]
